Storm Cap

A quick-on cover for the open-top GMC HUMMER EV, for when the panels are off and the truck sits outside: unpredictable weather, or a regular outdoor parking spot. It keeps rain out and takes the edge off cabin heat. Machine-washable, with removable, replaceable suction cups. Parked use only; it is not for driving.

Concept stage Parked use only SUV pattern: provisional Not yet tested on a truck Working choice: 8 cups (gate 3 confirms) Unit cost: placeholders, get quotes
Community pre-launch · GMC HUMMER EV owners

Panels off.
Worry off.

A lightweight, quick-on cover for the open-top HUMMER EV when you park outside with the panels off. Keeps the weather out and the heat down. Soft microfiber against the truck, no magnets, machine-washable, with replaceable suction cups. For parked use only. Help us shape it.

Concept stage · parked use onlyTake the 2-minute survey

Where this stands

Parked-only is the better product. It removes the driving-speed problem and makes washing, heat and tie-downs the real design questions. The idea is good; the blueprint still has holes that would hurt in front of owners, and they are all fixable.

Strong

Two benefits, one product

  • Open-top trucks that live outdoors need rain cover and sun cover. Selling both is stronger than selling rain alone, and it avoids implying a defect (GM does publish seal-alignment procedures for the Sky Panels: GM TechLink).
  • Washable with removable cups turns a fragile accessory into a maintained product.
  • Replacement cups become a repeat-purchase item (see Cost).
  • A first sewn prototype is a weekend and well under $150 in materials.
Blocks launch

Five things to prove or fix

  • Gusts and dwell time. Parked in a storm, cups alone rate to roughly 15–20 mph, and suction slowly loses grip over hours of heat cycling. Parked use makes backup tie-downs practical, so plan on them.
  • Side-window anchors. Frameless glass drops when a door opens, must seat in the roof seal, and loads cups in shear.
  • Heat claim. Black ripstop absorbs heat. You need a light or reflective outer option and a measured result before you say "cooler".
  • Washability. TPU laminate and seam tape can delaminate. Needs a 10-cycle wash test.
  • Credibility. Invented ISO claims are removed; the current renders show driving scenes and need to be redone.
Recommendation

8 glass cups + Gust Kit, gated

  • Cups position the cover and hold it in light wind. A removable Gust Kit of four straps to the running boards holds it in gusts: about 45–50 mph in the model at a 20° strap angle. Sold separately, so the base cover stays cheap.
  • Gate 8 glass cups on the door-open and seal-pinch tests. Fallback is 6 with B-pillar cups.
  • Print a tested gust rating on the label. "Storm Cap" implies a storm rating, so the label has to back the name.

6 vs 8: the anchor decision

Option A is 6 cups: 2 windshield, 2 B-pillar, 2 rear glass. Option B is 8 cups: 2 windshield, 4 side glass (front and rear doors), 2 rear glass. If that isn't how you meant them, tell me and I'll change the layouts.

Model and option drive the layout, pattern and cost below. SUV dimensions are placeholders until measured.
Cup on raked or horizontal-ish glass Cup on vertical side glass (shear-loaded) Cup on painted body
CriterionA · 6 cups, B-pillarB · 8 cups, side glass
Touches paintYes (B-pillar). Kills "zero paint contact".No. Glass only.
Modelled capacity——
Frameless glass drop on door openNot affectedRisk. Cups on the glass move or release when a door opens.
Glass-to-roof-seal pinchNot affectedRisk. Anything between glass and top seal can reopen the leak path (seal engagement spec is 4.5 mm ±1.5).
Load direction on cupMostly shear on a vertical pillarShear on vertical glass; normal on windshield and rear
Parts and cost6 cups, 6 straps8 cups, 8 straps: about 33% more hardware
Deploy timeFewer to press onTwo more per side, still quick
Airbag zonesKeep all straps off pillar trim and the roof-rail area. Check the owner's manual for curtain airbag deployment zones before choosing positions.

Wind-load model

Load = ½ρv² × lift coefficient × cover area. Capacity = cup pull, derated, then split into normal and shear for each glass angle. This is a first-order model with deliberately conservative defaults. A luggage-scale pull test on real glass (Roadmap gate 1) replaces the guesses.

Side glass is treated as 85° from horizontal (near vertical) and the B-pillar as 85°. Defaults: 350 N rated pull is about 80 lbf, a typical real-world figure for a 4.5 in. lever cup on clean glass. Ideal-vacuum math (what v1 used) is 2–3× higher and not achievable on wet, hot or aged glass. The dwell factor covers cups slowly losing vacuum over hours and heat cycles while parked; the 24/72-hour hold test (Roadmap gate 2) sets it. The Gust Kit defaults to 4 straps (two per side) at 500 N each, angled per the slider; only the vertical part of each strap resists uplift. Strap capacity is limited by the running-board mount, which you still need to verify. Set straps to 0 to see cups alone.

Max gust at your target safety factor, rounded down to 5 mph. The number on a label should come from your own test, not from this model.

How I'd decide

  • Run gates 1–4 on a real truck. Pull test, 24/72-hour hold, door-open glass drop, seal pinch.
  • Side glass passes: go 8, keep the glass-only claim.
  • Side glass fails or the seal pinches: go 6 with B-pillar cups on a clean-paint pad, add backup tie-downs, and change the copy to "no magnets".
  • Use the survey too. It asks owners which attach style they'd trust.

Pattern & construction

Flat pattern, redrawn to scale from the cover size entered above. 72 × 78 in. is a placeholder until you measure the truck. The measurement worksheet below captures what a pattern maker needs.

1 · Seams

Double flat-fell joins between panels A, B and C, folded inward so no raw edge sees rain. Bonded UV-resistant polyester thread.

2 · Seam sealing

The outer is a TPU-membrane laminate (target 10,000 mm). 22 mm TPU heat-seal tape goes over every seam, patch and vent edge. Seams and needle holes are the real leak paths, so test them (30-minute sprinkler soak plus a hose test).

3 · Hem and tension

1.5 in. double hem all round with 1/4 in. shock cord and corner cord-locks. Keep it snug so the edge doesn't flutter against the glass.

4 · Anchor points (removable)

Each anchor is a reinforced webbing tab (Box-X stitched 2 × 2 in. patch, 1 in. webbing) ending in a quick-release: the cup clips off in seconds with no tools, so the cover can go in the washer and a worn cup can be swapped. For the first runs use standard lever-lock cups on a side-release quick-release, which keeps cost down; a proprietary interface can wait. Sell spare cups. Colour-code front (red) and rear (black). Add a pull tab on each cup to break the vacuum, and tether each cup to the cover so a released cup can't drop and scratch anything. T1–T4 are optional backup tie-down points.

5 · Water management

Original plan put batten sleeves only in panels A and C. To crown the whole cover and shed water to both sides, run two side-to-side battens across the full width (drawn). Test pooling with a bucket pour.

6 · Wind relief

Two hooded mesh vents in panel B reduce trapped pressure. They also lower the lift coefficient in the load model, so measure it.

7 · Washable build

Battens sit in open-ended sleeves so they slide out, and the cups unclip. Target care: gentle cold cycle in a wash bag, no softener or bleach, line dry, no dryer (heat attacks TPU and seam tape). Re-treat the outer with a DWR spray if water stops beading. Print the care label, then prove it with a 10-cycle wash test.

8 · Heat and moisture

A dark outer absorbs sun and gets hot, which can soften cups on the glass beneath. Test a light grey or reflective-coated outer against black, same truck, same day. The breathable membrane and vents help stop condensation under a cover on a warm, humid truck. Measure before you claim a temperature drop.

9 · Gust Kit (removable running-board straps)

Four straps, two per side, sold separately. Each is 1 in. webbing with a side-release buckle, a microfiber sleeve over the middle, a padded loop or rubber-coated hook at the running-board end, and a clip to the cover's edge tab. A short fiberglass stand-off at the cover edge holds the strap away from the door paint (see the clearance check below). It blocks that door while fitted, so use one-handed releases. Confirm the running-board mount strength and finish before trusting it. Never fitted while driving.

Running-board strap clearance check

The roof is narrower than the doors, so a straight strap from the cover edge to the running board tends to ride on the door shoulder. This shows whether yours clears, and how far a stand-off at the cover edge must push the strap out. The defaults are placeholders. Measure the truck.

Cover edge half-width comes from the cover width above. Door shoulder is the widest point of the door side the strap would pass.

Truck measurement worksheet

Fill in on the truck, then give the numbers to whoever cuts the pattern. Saved in this browser. Do SUT and SUV separately; the roof footprint differs.

Seamstress pack

Everything a sewer needs to quote and build a prototype: cut list, layout, anchor map, materials, hardware, stitch spec, build order and checks. It reads the cover size, cup option and Gust Kit count from the workbook, so change those above and the pack updates. All sizes are placeholders until gate 0 (truck measured, muslin fitted).

Order of operations: send the pack and ask for a quote and a buildability review. Then have her cut a muslin test to your measurements, fit it on the truck, and update the numbers here. Only then cut real fabric. This is a first-pass spec from a non-sewer: she should be invited to change the construction.

Gen-2: bed canopy (SUT)

  
Your idea: flip the cover around, cups on the rear cab glass, and use it as shade over the bed when you're parked and hanging out or working back there. It's feasible, but as an accessory kit, not as the same cover with no changes.

  

    

      
    

    

      
Mini load check

      

        

        

        

      

      
Bed size is a placeholder; measure it. Uses the same cup, dwell, gust and safety inputs as the cover model above.

      

    

  


  

    
Works
Why it's worth it
  • Same fabric and cups, a second use, and a reflective outer doubles as bed shade.
  • The same 72 × 78 in. sheet is wider and longer than a typical bed, so it can reach the tailgate.
  • It fits how you use the truck: parked, outdoors, people in the bed.

    
Needs
What it can't do alone
  • Poles. There is no roof under it. Two or three bow or tent-style poles with rubber feet are needed to give headroom and stop pooling.
  • Bed anchors. Rear-glass cups only locate the front edge. Gusts need tie-downs to bed anchors, and their rating is unknown.
  • Bigger sail. Poles act as levers in wind, so rate it from a test.

    
Do now
Cheap choices to keep it open
  • Put D-rings or edge tabs on all four corners and mid-edges, so either end can be the front.
  • Add pole pockets or grommets at the corners.
  • Keep the rear-edge cups identical to the front ones.
  • Offer it as a "Shade Kit" add-on: 2–3 poles, 4 bed tie-downs, a bag.

  

  
Fastest test: use your gate 0 muslin template, drape it over the bed with two broom handles as poles, and see where the cups, edges and tie-downs want to go. About an afternoon. Never used while driving, and the tailgate must still work. This is SUT-only; an SUV has no open bed.

Roadmap to market

  
Gated so cheap tests kill bad ideas before expensive ones. Each gate has a pass/fail line.

  

    
0
Measure + paper template
Fill in the worksheet on a real truck. Cut a template from painter's plastic or muslin to check coverage, overhang and cup reach. Pass: the template covers the open roof with 5 in. past the side glass and every anchor reaches glass. Also fill in the strap clearance check with the truck's real body widths.

    
1
Cup pull test
Luggage scale, 3 cup models, on clean-dry, wet and sun-hot (130°F+) glass; windshield, side glass and rear glass. Record normal and shear pull. Pass: at or above the model's assumptions (350 N rated, 50% derate). Put your real numbers into the sliders.

    
2
Dwell test (24 / 72 hours)
Cups on glass in the sun, with a modest hanging load. Check grip at 0, 24 and 72 hours, through a rain and a heat cycle. Pass: grip stays at or above your dwell factor (0.7 in the model). Fail means re-pumpable cups or leaning harder on tie-downs.

    
3
Door-open / glass-drop test
With cups on the side glass, open and close each door. Pass: cups stay attached through a door cycle and nothing is pinched or released. Fail kills option B as drawn.

    
4
Seal-pinch test
Strap routing with the glass fully up. Pass: the window still seats in the top seal (cabin stays quiet and dry; GM's spec is 4.5 mm ±1.5 engagement) with the strap in place.

    
5
Sewn prototype + wet tests
2–3 units. Sprinkler soak 30 min plus a 2-minute hose test at every seam, patch and vent with dry paper towels under them, bucket pour for pooling, 4 hours in Florida sun. Time three people installing. Measure packed size against the under-seat space. Pass: dry cabin, no pooling, install under about 90 seconds, fits.

    
6
Gust-load test
Pick your target gust rating, read the load from the calculator, and pull each anchor group with a spring scale to that load for 5 minutes. Pass: no creep, no release, no seam damage. Print the label rating from what passes here, not from the model. For the running-board straps, also confirm the board mount is strong enough and that no buckle or hook ever touches paint.

    
7
Heat test
Same truck, same day, midday: covered vs uncovered, black outer vs light or reflective outer. Log cabin air, seat and dash surface temps with an IR thermometer or a cheap data logger for 3 hours. Pass: a difference big enough to state plainly. Quote only what you measured.

    
8
Wash test
Remove cups and battens, wash 10 cycles (gentle, cold, wash bag, line dry), then repeat the sprinkler soak and inspect seam tape and the TPU layer. Pass: no delamination, still sheds water (re-DWR if needed). Then write the care label.

    
9
Quick-release + replacement kit
Start with standard lever-lock cups on a side-release quick-release, which keeps first-run cost down. Swap a cup in under 15 seconds with no tools, cycle it 100 times, line up a second cup supplier, and define the spare-kit SKU. Pass: no wear or loosening, and a real kit cost for the Cost tab.

    
10
Business readiness
Product liability insurance quote, label warnings ("parked use only, not for driving"; "check cups and tie-downs before leaving the vehicle"), warranty and returns terms, trademark-safe naming, and a quick check with an attorney.

    
11
10-unit owner beta, then the 50-unit launch
Real owners, written feedback, photos of the actual product, then retire the renders. Collect responses with the survey (set an endpoint so submissions reach you).
